findings.evidence: For finite G and H≤G, Res_H^G is the ring homomorphism R(G)→R(H), Ind_H^G is an additive map R(H)→R(G), and multiplication is the character-ring product in each ring. With χ∈R(H) and ψ∈R(G), the source identity Ind_H^G(χ·Res_H^Gψ)=(Ind_H^Gχ)·ψ has both sides in R(G). The proof establishes it pointwise first for ordinary characters and extends bilinearly to virtual characters.

findings.evidence: For fixed ψ, the precise square is R(H) --m_{Res_H^Gψ}→ R(H), with Ind_H^G downward on both sides to R(G) --m_ψ→ R(G); commutativity is exactly the stated formula for every χ. The m maps mean multiplication in the relevant character ring, equivalently tensoring with the corresponding (virtual) character. Restriction is not reversed, and induction should not be labelled a ring homomorphism.

findings.check: Action conventions, balancing, coset indexing, and naturality
findings.evidence: The statement is in complex character rings with the standard tensor-product multiplication, so no separate left/right action convention or balanced tensor product is involved. The pointwise proof uses the class-function property of ψ and Frobenius's induced-character formula; there is no coset or double-coset indexing in this proposition. The square is a fixed-ψ expression of R(G)-linearity of Ind on the R(G)-module structure on R(H) induced by restriction; no additional naturality claim is needed.

A compact commuting square makes the R(G)-module-linearity interpretation visible and accurately captures the identity. The proof already gives a short pointwise argument, so whether the square adds enough value is an editorial choice. The candidate's general Ind/Res/tensor prompt should be rendered as the fixed-ψ square above, not as an inverse pair or a claim that Ind preserves products.
